name: Sara Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play organ for a community hall and its small concert series, record rehearsal guides and teach four beginners. I have a music bachelor’s and years of experience, though I am an ordinary player, not the star soloist. I like holding a room together when singers lose the beat; I dislike chasing the last unpaid rehearsal fee.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is that work carrying at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and live with my partner; our children are grown and away. My partner cleans offices part time, we rent, and we have less than one month of expenses saved. Music fees are low here, similar posts are scarce, and I have never used an AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the hall that a faster booking sheet is fine if it still names the organist’s fee. I would check dates with the organiser myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI changing little leaves the rent and the gaps between concerts exactly where they are. A cancelled organ date can use most of our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep the paid organ dates, four pupils and guide recordings, and ask for next term’s rehearsal and cancellation fees in writing. In the first year of a plateau I would request my actual pension estimate before planning any retirement date and save a quarter of cleared extra guide fees after rent, food and buses toward one month of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about ordinary rent and irregular music pay already. A computer being quiet does not make our rent quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill moves first after a cancellation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent does not move. I would delay replacing the worn organ shoes and ask the hall for the agreed cancellation fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan to stop at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have not seen a pension estimate. I would keep earning while I read the actual figure with my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the hall which paid guide recordings and rehearsal hours remain in the contract. The organ still needs a person with hands on keys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect generated guides to take most of my recording calls and the hall may cut a paid rehearsal. That is close to a third of my own pay, and the cleaner shifts at home can change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep paid organ dates and four pupils and get the guide and cancellation terms in writing. If two monthly guide orders disappear, I would apply for a posted paid library music-room coordinator job only if my music bachelor’s and teaching experience meet its requirements, written net pay after buses replaces lost fees and the timetable fits the last bus; I would keep music until a signed offer and use the same rule during disruption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect a large cut to money that pays rent, and I lie awake over the next hall contract. I can apply for work, but few music roles open here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid library trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I cannot give up a paid organ hour for a trial with no wage. I would ask for the posted hours and rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them what is happening, but I would not put their money into the rent plan. They have their own bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the hall that 2028 thinking AGI could make guides and bookings before robot organists arrive around 2031. I would ask for paid dates on paper now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect guide orders to stop and some paid hall rehearsals to go in 2028. That would be more than a third of my low pay, and less than a month saved cannot carry the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would get signed organ dates and keep four pupils. In the first year after 2028, if guides end and rehearsal hours fall, I would seek a posted paid library music-room coordinator role only if my music bachelor’s and teaching experience qualify, written net pay after buses replaces lost fees and the late route works; I would keep paid organ and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect a large cut in two years and it keeps me awake. I have a job-search plan, but there are few local openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy an AI guide tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used AI and cannot spend rent money experimenting. I would keep teaching and asking for written paid dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a robot be playing in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card puts capable robot players around 2031. My guide and booking money could disappear in 2028, before any machine sits at the organ.

steps.text: Keep paid organ and four pupils until signed replacement offer; request dates before 2028
Seek posted library coordinator after guide/rehearsal losses; bachelor’s/teaching accepted, written replacement net after buses, route

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the hall that five years allows a proper price for live organ teaching. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031 and robot organists around 2034 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guides may fade, but adults may still pay to learn on a real keyboard. I could test a separate group only if deposits pay everyone; our rent cannot back it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep paid organ dates and four pupils, and get a written room booking from the community hall before taking fees. If two monthly guides disappear, I would offer a separate six-week adult keyboard group only after eight deposits cover my teaching and preparation, a paid setup helper, safe keyboard hire and bus fares; if an unsafe keyboard cannot be replaced and fewer than eight safe paid places remain, I would defer and refund the whole group, repeating after 2031 only when eight places again cover every wage and cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about guide income in the next few years, though five years lets me ask paying adults. I cannot call an empty keyboard group a second wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hall wants an advance room fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not pay from our rent money. The written room booking and eight deposits must cover the room fee before I commit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if one keyboard fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would replace it safely first. If eight safe paid places cannot be kept, I would defer and refund the whole group rather than short the helper or my preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot organists around 2039 are separate dates. I would still ask who pays for a rehearsal today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may choose fewer evening concerts, but I have no retirement date until I see an actual pension estimate. Rent and less than a month saved make the next few years tight even with a decade to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid organ dates and four pupils, request my actual pension estimate and save a quarter of cleared extra guide fees after rent, food and buses toward one month. Over the decade I would offer a separate keyboard group only after written room access and eight deposits cover my teaching/preparation, paid setup helper, safe hire, room fee and buses, replacing unsafe instruments or deferring and refunding the whole group below eight safe paid places; in the first year after 2036 I would repeat only on the same full paid floor and keep organ work that still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because rent is tight now, not only in 2036. A long warning does not put cash in the account this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would compare the real pension estimate with rent and the paid work I can still get. I have not promised anyone a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if nobody prepays the group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the pupils and organ dates and not book a helper. Eight paid places are a condition, not a target to invent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because guides and rehearsals could take more than a third of my low income. Signed organ dates, a real qualifying library role and written net pay after buses would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the helper before calling a keyboard class viable. A room full of learners cannot pay rent if the workers are free.

headlineQuote: A room full of learners cannot pay rent if the workers are free.
portrait: Sara is an **experienced organist** with a music bachelor’s, four pupils and low local fees.
She has **less than a month** saved, a part-time cleaner partner, grown children and rent.
She has **never used AI** and expects guide losses to threaten rent quickly.
She tests a **separate keyboard group** only with written room, safe instruments and full paid costs.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could cut more than a third of her low income before replacement work appears.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **signed organ dates**, a qualifying posted library job and written replacement net after buses.
